paragraphs: Adversarial risk measures classification error when an adversary can manipulate test inputs. This paper asks about the best error rate any classifier could achieve under such interference. That changes the focus from improving a particular defense to understanding limits imposed by the classification problem itself.

For binary classification with a zero–one loss, which counts predictions as either correct or incorrect, the authors characterize optimal adversarial risk through an optimal transport cost between the two class distributions. A suitably chosen transport cost makes this connection exact. They also introduce a coupling strategy that attains the transport optimum for several one-dimensional distributions, including Gaussian, uniform, and triangular distributions.

Those couplings let the authors derive optimal adversarial classifiers in the studied settings and examine how they differ from classifiers optimized without adversaries. The analysis also supports evaluations of algorithm-independent risk limits for several image datasets and related Gaussian mixtures. These results provide a way to study achievable robustness through the relationship between class distributions.
icml-2020-adversarial-risk-via-optimal-t.tldr: The paper characterizes optimal binary adversarial risk using optimal transport and derives optimal robust classifiers for several one-dimensional distributions.

paragraphs: Influence maximization concerns choosing people whose participation helps information spread through a network. Many formulations restrict how many influencers can be selected. This paper instead considers the total cost of an advertising campaign, addressing the practical fact that different influencers can charge different amounts.

The resulting online framework asks how to obtain value from an overall advertising budget while learning about influence. A spending constraint changes which choices are attractive: the number of selected influencers alone does not capture their affordability. The proposed algorithm assumes an independent cascade model of diffusion and edge-level semi-bandit feedback, so its analysis depends on a particular spreading model and access to feedback about individual network edges.

The paper provides both theoretical and experimental results for this budgeted approach. Its analysis also applies to the more familiar setting that limits the number of selected influencers, where it improves the stated best available regret bound. Thus, the contribution includes both a more cost-sensitive problem formulation and a stronger learning guarantee for an existing formulation.
icml-2020-budgeted-online-influence-maxi.tldr: A budget-based influence-maximization framework accounts for differing influencer costs and improves the regret bound for the cardinality-constrained setting.

paragraphs: Very deep convolutional networks commonly use normalization and skip connections alongside careful initialization. This paper investigates whether deep networks can still train effectively without the first two techniques. It reports strong image-recognition performance from plain convolutional networks when their layers are encouraged to behave nearly isometrically.

An isometric transformation preserves geometric size and distance. The method keeps convolution kernels close to this behavior both at initialization and throughout training. It also modifies the ReLU activation by shifting it toward being isometric. The approach therefore coordinates the behavior of the convolutional transformations and the nonlinear activation, rather than relying on initialization alone.

The experiments show that deep networks without normalization or skip connections can perform well on standard recognition benchmarks. When skip connections are added, the near-isometric networks match standard ResNet performance on ImageNet and exceed it on COCO, while still using no normalization. These findings establish a successful alternative in the evaluated settings and challenge the belief that normalization and skip connections are indispensable for training deep convolutional networks.
icml-2020-deep-isometric-learning-for-vi.tldr: Keeping convolutional layers near isometric enables strong visual recognition with deep networks that omit normalization and, in some experiments, skip connections.

paragraphs: Some health measurements, particularly those produced by high-throughput sequencing, are compositional: interpreting one feature depends on the other features in the sample. This dependence complicates both prediction and explanation. An attribution that ignores it may fail to respect the structure of the data being analyzed.

DeepCoDA addresses this issue with a framework for high-dimensional compositional health data. It also targets personalized interpretability, defined here as attributing a model's conclusion to features for an individual sample. The architecture uses patient-specific weights to provide these individualized explanations while maintaining coherence with the compositional nature of the inputs.

Across 25 real-world datasets, the authors report performance at the state of the art together with personalized, compositionally coherent interpretations. The contribution is therefore a combination of predictive modeling and explanations appropriate to the measurement structure. This matters for precision health because domain experts need to assess the relevance and reliability of a particular patient's prediction, including whether its interpretation reflects biology rather than technical preprocessing choices.
icml-2020-deepcoda-personalized-interpre.tldr: DeepCoDA combines competitive prediction on compositional health data with patient-specific explanations that respect dependencies among features.

paragraphs: Overparameterized neural networks can fit their training data perfectly while still making relatively few errors on new examples. Explaining this combination remains difficult. One proposed route uses PAC-Bayes bounds, which relate predictive performance to distributions over models, and optimizes those bounds using variational inference.

This paper examines the mean-field version of that approach. Here, the posterior distribution is represented by a Gaussian with diagonal covariance, so it does not represent correlations between model parameters. The authors empirically find that optimizing PAC-Bayes bounds within this restricted family produces negligible gains. Their investigation concerns how useful this particular approximation is for obtaining informative generalization guarantees.

The authors also examine possible explanations involving optimization difficulties in variational inference and a poorly chosen prior. Their results suggest that richer posterior distributions are the most promising direction for further progress. This is an empirical diagnosis and a research recommendation: the findings motivate reconsidering the distributional approximation used to describe trained networks, rather than establishing that every mean-field method must fail.
icml-2020-dissecting-non-vacuous-general.tldr: An empirical study finds negligible gains from mean-field variational PAC-Bayes bounds and points toward richer posterior distributions.

paragraphs: Domain generalization asks a model to perform well in environments it did not encounter during training. Training domains can contain useful shared patterns alongside patterns specific to each domain. Common Specific Decomposition, or CSD, explicitly gives these two kinds of information separate components during learning.

The method jointly learns a common component intended to generalize and domain-specific components that fit the training domains. After training, it discards the domain-specific components and retains only the common one. Implementation requires changing just the final linear classification layer of a neural network. The paper also analyzes identifiability, meaning whether the decomposition can be determined, and studies how low-rank structure affects generalization.

In the reported evaluations, CSD matches or exceeds approaches based on domain erasure, domain-perturbed augmentation, and meta-learning. Diagnostics using rotated MNIST support the hypothesis that it separates common information from domain-specific information. Together, these findings suggest that explicitly accommodating training-domain peculiarities can help isolate the component useful for unseen domains, with a relatively small architectural modification.
icml-2020-efficient-domain-generalizatio.tldr: CSD separates shared and domain-specific classifier components during training, then keeps the shared component to generalize to unseen domains.

paragraphs: A low-dimensional representation can reveal groups of data points, but seeing a group does not explain what distinguishes its members. This paper treats the next step—understanding differences between groups—as an interpretation problem. It uses the model that produced the representation to help identify those differences.

The authors introduce Global Counterfactual Explanations and an algorithm called Transitive Global Translations to compute them. The algorithm uses compressed sensing to identify relatively sparse differences between pairs of groups. It also requires those pairwise explanations to agree across the full collection of groups, so each comparison participates in a consistent account of the representation.

Experiments show that the resulting explanations can accurately describe the model while involving relatively few differences, and that they correspond to real patterns in the data. This connects visual grouping with a more concrete explanation of what the learned representation captures. The consistency requirement matters because users often compare several groups together, and separate explanations are less useful if they fail to fit into a coherent overall picture.
icml-2020-explaining-groups-of-points-in.tldr: Transitive Global Translations explains groups in learned representations through sparse pairwise differences that remain consistent across groups.

paragraphs: Few-shot relation extraction identifies the relationship between two entities in a sentence using only a small number of labeled examples per relation. This paper seeks better generalization to new relations by using information about how different relations are connected. It represents that information in a global relation graph.

The method gives each relation a prototype vector and learns a posterior distribution over these prototypes. A graph neural network operating on the relation graph parameterizes their initial prior. This lets the graph inform what the model expects before adapting to the available examples, while the posterior represents uncertainty about the resulting relation prototypes.

To optimize these distributions, the authors use stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics, which they relate to MAML while emphasizing its ability to handle prototype uncertainty. The complete framework supports efficient end-to-end optimization. Experiments on two benchmark datasets demonstrate effectiveness against competitive baselines in both few-shot and zero-shot settings. The central contribution is bringing relation structure and uncertainty together when direct labeled evidence for a relation is scarce.
icml-2020-few-shot-relation-extraction-v.tldr: A relation graph supplies Bayesian priors for uncertain relation prototypes, improving extraction when labeled examples are scarce or absent.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor search finds data points close to a query. Graph-based methods have been successful empirically, but their practical success has had relatively little theoretical support. This paper develops rigorous analysis to help explain the performance of these methods and the effects of commonly used search heuristics.

The analysis focuses on low-dimensional data, specifically when dimension d is much smaller than log n, where n is the number of points. It examines a basic greedy search on nearest-neighbor graphs as well as two practical modifications. Shortcut edges aim to accelerate movement through the graph, while a changing list of candidate points is used to improve search accuracy.

The authors support their theoretical investigation with experimental analysis. By considering both the basic algorithm and practical modifications, the work connects mathematical understanding with choices made in working search systems. Its stated dimensional regime is important to interpreting the contribution: the analysis offers insight into benefits and limits of graph search within that setting, rather than claiming a general guarantee across all dimensions.
icml-2020-graph-based-nearest-neighbor-s.tldr: The paper analyzes graph-based nearest-neighbor search and common speed and accuracy heuristics in a low-dimensional regime.

paragraphs: Boosting builds a classifier by combining predictive components. This paper explores a non-convex approach to that task using integer programming. Its central question is practical as well as mathematical: whether this optimization route can support useful classification methods while addressing shortcomings of convex boosting approaches.

Integer programming makes discrete optimization decisions part of the formulation. IPBoost uses this machinery to pursue non-convex boosting, placing the choice of optimization formulation at the center of the contribution. The work presents that choice as a way to circumvent shortcomings associated with convex alternatives, and demonstrates that the resulting approach is practical on real-world problems.

The reported classification results are comparable to or better than the state of the art. Their significance is that the non-convex integer-programming route is supported by practical results, rather than appearing only as a possible formulation. The evidence therefore supports IPBoost as a competitive approach in the evaluated settings, with the contribution spanning both the optimization method and its demonstrated applicability to classification.
icml-2020-ipboost-non-convex-boosting-vi.tldr: IPBoost uses integer programming for non-convex boosting and reports practical classification results comparable to or better than the state of the art.

paragraphs: Neural networks with discrete random variables cannot be trained by directly differentiating through those variables in the usual way. Gradient estimators provide a workaround, but their accuracy and variability affect learning. This paper focuses on networks whose latent variables are Boolean, taking one of two possible values.

The authors use harmonic analysis of Boolean functions to derive analytic expressions for the bias and variance of the Straight-Through estimator. Bias concerns systematic error in the estimated gradient, while variance concerns how much estimates fluctuate. These expressions guide the design of FouST, an estimator intended to keep both quantities low while retaining the efficiency of Straight-Through estimation.

The motivation is especially relevant to hierarchical stochastic networks, where efficient estimators such as Straight-Through and Gumbel-Softmax can lose effectiveness. Extensive experiments report that FouST compares favorably with state-of-the-art biased estimators and is much faster than unbiased alternatives. The contribution links a mathematical diagnosis of gradient-estimation error to an efficient algorithm, with experimental support for the resulting trade-off.
icml-2020-low-bias-low-variance-gradient.tldr: FouST uses an analysis of Boolean functions to build efficient gradient estimates with low bias and variance for stochastic networks.

paragraphs: In long-horizon reinforcement learning, an agent's eventual goals may be too distant to provide useful feedback early in training. Repeatedly attempting those goals can leave the agent without a productive learning signal. This paper asks which goals the agent should choose for itself while developing the capabilities needed to reach farther.

The proposed objective increases the entropy of the distribution of goals achieved so far, encouraging broader coverage of achieved outcomes. The agent pursues previously achieved goals in sparsely explored parts of goal space. This focuses training near the frontier of what it can already accomplish, using reachable outcomes to direct further exploration.

The authors report an order-of-magnitude improvement in sample efficiency over the prior state of the art on evaluated long-horizon multi-goal tasks, including maze navigation and block stacking. The finding supports choosing training goals according to current exploration history when desired test-time goals offer little guidance. It also gives a concrete objective for selecting intermediate goals, connecting their usefulness to expanded coverage of achievable outcomes.
icml-2020-maximum-entropy-gain-explorati.tldr: Choosing previously achieved goals in sparsely explored regions improves sample efficiency on evaluated long-horizon multi-goal tasks.

paragraphs: This paper develops exact convex representations of training two-layer ReLU neural networks. A convex formulation offers a different mathematical description of the training problem, and exactness means the connection is an equivalence rather than an approximation. The stated convex program has a number of variables polynomial in the training-sample count and hidden-neuron count.

The theory uses semi-infinite duality and minimum-norm regularization. One central result identifies ReLU networks trained with standard weight decay with convex models using a block l1 penalty. This connects regularization of neural-network weights to a structured penalty in another model representation, helping explain what the training objective is selecting.

The paper also establishes that certain standard linear convolutional networks correspond to semidefinite programs. These can be simplified further into l1-regularized linear models in a discrete Fourier feature space of polynomial size. Together, the results reveal exact relationships between the specified network-training problems and established convex formulations. Their scope is the two-layer ReLU and particular linear convolutional settings described, so the architectural conditions are central to the interpretation.
icml-2020-neural-networks-are-convex-reg.tldr: The paper gives exact convex formulations for two-layer ReLU training and connects certain linear convolutional networks to regularized Fourier-feature models.

paragraphs: With a constant step size, stochastic gradient descent can first move rapidly toward an optimum and later fluctuate around it. These phases call for different behavior: a step size that supports early progress can become too large for continued refinement. This paper studies detecting that transition to guide step-size reductions.

The authors analyze a classical statistical test based on inner products between successive stochastic gradients. They show that it cannot provide an adequate convergence diagnostic even for a quadratic objective. This matters because the test attempts to infer progress from readily available gradient information, yet its behavior is insufficient even in that simple setting.

The paper then proposes a different, simple statistical procedure that accurately detects stationarity. It shows that efficiently detecting the transition and appropriately decreasing the step size can yield fast convergence rates. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report state-of-the-art performance. The contribution combines a diagnosis of an existing test with a replacement procedure, connecting statistical monitoring of optimization to decisions about how large future updates should be.
icml-2020-on-convergence-diagnostic-base.tldr: A new stationarity diagnostic guides SGD step-size reductions after showing that a classical gradient-based test is inadequate even for quadratic objectives.

paragraphs: For monotone submodular maximization with a limit on the number of selected items, the standard greedy algorithm guarantees a worst-case approximation factor of 1−1/e. Such problems have diminishing returns: an item's extra value can shrink as more items are selected. Yet empirical performance often substantially exceeds the worst-case guarantee.

This paper introduces sharpness for submodular functions as a candidate explanation for that gap. The authors prove that the greedy algorithm's performance improves as the function's sharpness increases. This gives a way to express stronger guarantees using additional structure in the objective, rather than evaluating every problem solely through the same worst-case factor.

The result also connects greedy selection to convex optimization, where sharpness is associated with faster convergence of first-order methods. That relationship places improved greedy behavior within a broader mathematical pattern. Sharpness is presented as a candidate explanation for observed effectiveness, and the theorem establishes a specific link between that property and improved guarantees under the stated submodular, monotone, cardinality-constrained setting.
icml-2020-on-the-unreasonable-effectiven.tldr: A sharpness property yields stronger guarantees for greedy submodular maximization and offers a candidate explanation for its strong practical performance.

paragraphs: Unbalanced optimal transport compares measures that may have different total masses. This paper analyzes the computational cost of using the Sinkhorn algorithm for an entropy-regularized version of that problem. Each measure has at most n components, and the analysis asks how work grows as the desired approximation error ε decreases.

The authors establish a complexity bound of approximately n²/ε, with logarithmic factors suppressed. They contrast this with the cited best known Sinkhorn upper bound for standard optimal transport, approximately n²/ε² under the same notation. The distinction is in the dependence on accuracy: the unbalanced bound grows more slowly as ε becomes smaller.

The proof combines geometric convergence of the updates toward the optimal dual solution with scaling properties of the primal solution. It differs from the analysis for standard transport because the unbalanced solution need not satisfy exact marginal constraints. The result provides a computational guarantee for the unbalanced problem and explains how its mathematical structure supports a different proof and a better stated accuracy dependence.
icml-2020-on-unbalanced-optimal-transpor.tldr: The paper establishes a roughly n²/ε Sinkhorn complexity bound for unbalanced optimal transport using convergence and scaling properties.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether a classifier can provide optimal robustness against every adversarial attack. It formulates attack and defense as an infinite zero-sum game, where an advantage for one side is a disadvantage for the other. In this setting, familiar equilibrium theorems do not directly apply.

The authors show that their game has no Nash equilibrium when both the classifier and adversary are deterministic. This yields a negative answer to the motivating question in that regime. They also show that any deterministic classifier can be outperformed by a randomized classifier within their framework. Whether optimal robustness against all attacks is achievable in the randomized regime remains open.

These results motivate a simple method for constructing randomized classifiers. Experiments support the theoretical analysis and show stronger performance than adversarial training against strong adaptive attacks. Under the reported adaptive PGD attack on CIFAR10, the method achieves accuracy of 0.55 compared with 0.42 for adversarial training. This provides concrete evidence for randomization as a defense strategy while preserving the unresolved status of the broader optimality question.
icml-2020-randomization-matters-how-to-d.tldr: Game-theoretic analysis and adaptive-attack experiments support randomized defenses, while universal optimal robustness in the randomized regime remains unresolved.

paragraphs: One-bit compressed sensing seeks to recover a signal from noisy measurements quantized to a single bit. This paper assumes the target is generated from a k-dimensional representation by a known n-layer ReLU network producing a d-dimensional output. The network supplies low-dimensional structure without requiring a known sparsity basis.

Recovery uses unconstrained empirical risk minimization. Under a sub-exponential measurement assumption, the authors prove uniform recovery to error ε using roughly kn log d/ε² measurements, suppressing additional logarithmic factors. For shallow networks, this matches the information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors in inverse accuracy. Uniformity means the guarantee covers any target represented by the specified generator.

The paper also studies the non-convex optimization landscape. Under suitable conditions on network weights, stationary points are confined to small neighborhoods of the true representation and a negative multiple of it. Further weight assumptions place the global minimizer near the true representation. These conditional results connect measurement requirements with favorable landscape structure, while distinguishing the statistical guarantee from the additional conditions needed for the computational conclusions.
icml-2020-robust-one-bit-recovery-via-re.tldr: A known ReLU generator enables conditional uniform recovery guarantees from noisy one-bit measurements, alongside analysis of the non-convex recovery landscape.

paragraphs: Large reinforcement-learning experiments often depend on distributed systems and expensive hardware. Sample Factory addresses this access problem by improving efficiency and resource use within a single machine. Its goal is to make demanding training workloads faster through the design of the training system itself.

The architecture combines an asynchronous sampler running on a GPU with off-policy correction techniques. These pieces support rapid collection and use of experience while accounting for the off-policy aspect of training. On non-trivial three-dimensional control problems, the system achieves more than 100,000 environment frames per second without sacrificing sample efficiency. This separates processing experience quickly from needing more experience to learn.

The authors also extend the system to support self-play and population-based training, then use those capabilities to train highly capable agents for a multiplayer first-person shooter. The contribution therefore includes both a high-throughput single-machine architecture and support for more elaborate training setups. The stated results show how better use of available computation can expand the scale of reinforcement-learning experiments.
icml-2020-sample-factory-egocentric-3d-c.tldr: Sample Factory exceeds 100,000 environment frames per second on 3D control tasks using efficient asynchronous reinforcement learning on a single machine.

paragraphs: Differentiable physics makes physical simulation usable within gradient-based learning and control. Scaling such methods becomes difficult when many objects interact. This paper develops a framework designed to support large numbers of objects while accommodating arbitrary object geometry and topology through mesh representations.

The framework exploits sparse contacts: collision handling can focus on localized regions instead of introducing optimization variables across the whole scene. This keeps the number of collision-related variables smaller even when many objects are simulated. The authors also accelerate implicit differentiation through optimization problems with nonlinear constraints, addressing the cost of obtaining derivatives as well as resolving physical interactions.

Experiments report reductions of up to two orders of magnitude in both memory and computation compared with recent particle-based methods. Evaluations on inverse problems and control scenarios also report performance improvements of at least an order of magnitude over derivative-free and model-free baselines. These results support localized collision handling and faster differentiation as useful ingredients for scaling the evaluated physics-based learning and control problems.
icml-2020-scalable-differentiable-physic.tldr: Mesh-based localized collision handling and faster implicit differentiation substantially reduce the cost of differentiable physics in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper addresses three linked goals for deep neural networks: preserving differential privacy, maintaining useful predictions, and providing certified robustness against adversarial examples. These goals interact, so the proposed method treats their trade-offs as part of the training design rather than considering privacy and robustness separately.

The mechanism randomizes both inputs and latent representations. It uses sequential composition in differential privacy to combine these operations and strengthen robustness bounds. The authors also design an adversarial objective using the post-processing property of differential privacy, aiming to tighten model sensitivity while addressing predictive utility, privacy loss, and robustness together.

For scalability, the paper introduces stochastic batch training that bypasses the conventional iterative batch-by-batch approach used in differentially private neural-network training. End-to-end theoretical analysis and evaluations report notable improvements in robustness and scalability. The contribution combines a mechanism for certified protection with a training procedure intended for large networks and datasets, making the relationship between privacy accounting, robustness guarantees, and practical training cost central to the approach.
icml-2020-scalable-differential-privacy-.tldr: The method combines input and latent randomization with a new training procedure to improve scalability and certified robustness in differentially private networks.

paragraphs: An agent that needs many skills cannot conveniently rely on a separately engineered reward for every skill. Setting its own goals offers an alternative, but the goal-selection rule still needs a principled objective. This paper proposes maximizing state coverage for policies trained to reach goals defined by full state observations.

The authors show that this objective is equivalent to combining goal-reaching performance with high entropy in the goal distribution. Skew-Fit implements the goal-distribution part of this principle. Under regularity conditions, it converges to a uniform distribution over valid states even when the set of valid states is initially unknown. The conditions are part of the convergence claim.

When paired with existing goal-reaching methods, Skew-Fit outperforms several prior approaches on the evaluated visual goal-reaching tasks. The paper also demonstrates a real robot learning to open a door from pixels, starting from scratch and without a manually designed reward. These results connect a formal coverage objective to practical self-supervised skill learning, with goal selection providing the mechanism for encouraging broader experience.
icml-2020-skew-fit-state-covering-self-s.tldr: Skew-Fit learns diverse self-generated goals, with conditional state-coverage guarantees and demonstrations of visual skill learning without manually designed rewards.

paragraphs: The argsort operation returns the permutation that puts a vector's entries in sorted order. Its output is discrete, so its gradients are zero almost everywhere. This creates an obstacle when a model needs to learn through a sorting decision using ordinary end-to-end gradient-based training.

SoftSort replaces that discrete operation with a continuous relaxation. Such a replacement provides a way to incorporate sorting-related behavior into differentiable models. The paper's emphasis is simplicity: the proposed relaxation can be implemented in three lines of code and has mathematical structure that makes it easier to reason about and substantially simplifies proofs.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance and faster computation than competing approaches. These findings matter because a relaxation has to be both useful for learning and practical to compute; a complicated substitute can make sorting-based models harder to build and analyze. SoftSort brings implementation simplicity, mathematical tractability, and empirical competitiveness together in one operator. The authors also release code for reproducing their experiments and results.
icml-2020-softsort-a-continuous-relaxati.tldr: SoftSort offers a simple continuous approximation to argsort that supports gradient-based learning and runs faster than competing approaches.

paragraphs: Speech carries information about language content, timbre, pitch, and rhythm. Separating these components would make them easier to analyze or modify independently. Existing voice-conversion systems described in the paper separate timbre, but leave content, pitch, and rhythm entangled in the remaining representation.

The difficulty is that separating those remaining components without explicit annotations is underdetermined: the available speech does not by itself specify a unique decomposition. SpeechSplit addresses this challenge with three carefully designed information bottlenecks. These restrictions on information flow enable the system to decompose speech into the four components without labels specifying each one.

The resulting system can separately transfer timbre, pitch, and rhythm styles without text labels, placing it among the first algorithms with that capability. This matters because independent control over those aspects requires representations that distinguish them, rather than treating all non-timbre information as one bundle. The contribution is a concrete architecture for achieving that separation while avoiding the difficult and expensive component-level annotations that would otherwise help specify the task.
icml-2020-unsupervised-speech-decomposit.tldr: SpeechSplit uses three information bottlenecks to separate speech content, timbre, pitch, and rhythm without text labels.

paragraphs: WaveFlow is a compact generative model for raw audio trained directly by maximum likelihood. It combines a dilated two-dimensional convolutional architecture for long-range waveform structure with autoregressive functions for local variation. This design addresses both broad temporal organization and fine changes in the audio signal.

The framework includes WaveNet and WaveGlow as special cases, providing a shared perspective on likelihood-based models for one-dimensional data. WaveFlow needs only a few sequential generation steps even for waveforms with hundreds of thousands of time steps. The authors report speech fidelity comparable to WaveNet with synthesis several orders of magnitude faster, and a substantial reduction in the likelihood gap between autoregressive and efficient flow-based models.

The reported model contains 5.91 million parameters, making it 15 times smaller than WaveGlow. On a V100 GPU, it generates 22.05 kHz audio at 42.6 times real time without engineered inference kernels. These findings connect compact model size, rapid generation, and high-fidelity speech within the evaluated setup, illustrating the benefits of combining flow-based generation with expressive local autoregressive modeling.
icml-2020-waveflow-a-compact-flow-based-.tldr: WaveFlow combines long-range convolutions and local autoregressive modeling to generate high-fidelity speech quickly with a compact flow-based model.
